Remember what a shrinking clear zone means. As resistant bacteria survive and multiply, they grow closer to the disc, so the measured diameter gets smaller over the 5 days.
walkthrough:
**Understand what the zone tells us**

Think of the clear zone as the no-grow area around the antibiotic disc. A large zone means the antibiotic is killing bacteria well.

Rule from the question:
$$zone < 13.0\ mm = resistant\ bacteria\ present$$

**Check each type against the 13.0 mm threshold**

Now scan the table, especially day 5, when resistance has had time to show.

Type 1 day 5 = $14.3\ mm$ (still above 13.0, so not resistant). Type 2 day 5 = $2.0\ mm$, Type 3 day 5 = $10.9\ mm$, Type 4 day 5 = $2.0\ mm$ (all below 13.0, so resistant). Type 5 day 5 = $20.4\ mm$ (well above 13.0, so not resistant).

**Pick the statement the data actually supports**

Only types 2, 3 and 4 fall below $13.0\ mm$. Types 1 and 5 stay above it for all 5 days. That matches option B exactly, and it avoids claiming too much about the future or about treatment.

options.A: Not true for all types. Types 1 (14.3 mm) and 5 (20.4 mm) are still above 13.0 mm on day 5, so they do not show resistance in this data.
options.B: Correct. Types 2, 3 and 4 all drop below 13.0 mm by day 5, while types 1 and 5 stay above 13.0 mm throughout.
options.C: Incorrect. Type 3 drops to 10.9 mm, so it shows resistance, and type 5 stays at 20.4 mm, so the antibiotic still works well on it.
options.D: Too strong a claim. The data only shows 5 days with no resistance yet for type 5, it cannot prove what can never happen in the future.
